244: And all of it was done in your name.
245: For the Hōgen New Code, see the Hyōhanki, entry for Hōgen 1, intercalary 9th month, 18th day. The uneven distribution of rewards was a distant cause of the Heiji Disturbance; see the Heiji Monogatari.
246: Follow Shinzei's plan: reward the Taira generously, the Minamoto sparingly
247: Grant Yoshitomo more, and give him a provincial governorship
248: The Minamoto's hearts may be won, but the Taira may take offence
249: Reward both houses, and expand the Emperor's Northern Guard
250: Never hand the hilt of the sword to a single house
254: You hear that at the post-station of Aohaka in Mino there lives an old woman named *Otomae*, past seventy, a true heir of the imayō tradition who received the authentic teaching of the master Mei.
255: You send an envoy to fetch her. She arrives stooped, her hair white as frost, and bows her head to the floor below the dais: “This old one has not sung in many years. Only the voice of a withered tree is left in my throat.”
256: Yet the moment she opens her mouth, the hall falls silent. It is an ancient melody unlike anything you have heard—unadorned, like a mountain stream. Listening behind the blinds, you feel your eyes grow hot.
257: “Your Majesty's voice is too bright. Imayō must be sung like a river, not like a bell.”
258: “Then I ask you, Teacher—teach me to be a river.”
259: The Son of Heaven has taken a singing woman as his teacher, and not one noble at court knows how to record it in his diary.
260: Go-Shirakawa's taking Otomae as his teacher is recorded in the Ryōjin Hishō Kudenshū, Book 10. Otomae died in Kaō 1 (1169); Go-Shirakawa visited her on her deathbed, chanting sutras and singing imayō for her.
261: Observe the courtesies of a disciple, and learn the old style in full
262: This will be the most earnest discipline of your life
263: Summon Otomae to the palace, and entertain your favourites with an imayō banquet
264: Song, too, is an art of winning hearts
268: In the 8th month of Hōgen 3, you abdicate in favour of sixteen-year-old Morihito, who becomes *Emperor Nijō*. The matter was settled between Bifukumon-in and Shinzei—people called it “a council of Buddha with Buddha,” for both had taken holy orders. You move to Sanjō-dono and become the *Retired Emperor*.
269: With the beginning of cloistered rule, a young favourite appears at your side: *Fujiwara no Nobuyori*. Barely past twenty, graceful and at ease, he enjoys your lavish favour, rising within a few years from Middle Captain of the Right Inner Palace Guards to Provisional Middle Counsellor. Yet Nobuyori is not content. He asks to be made *Major Captain of the Inner Palace Guards*.
270: Shinzei opposes it flatly. One day he presents you with a picture scroll depicting Emperor Xuanzong of Tang and the Consort Yang—the rebellion of An Lushan, the slope at Mawei, Yuhuan strangled. At its end is an inscription in Shinzei's own hand: may Your Majesty take this as a warning, and not favour ministers without talent.
271: “An Lushan was but a barbarian youth, yet Xuanzong favoured him, and it ended at Mawei. I beg Your Majesty to look upon this scroll and think thrice.”
272: “Does the Lay Priest mean to liken me to Lushan?” Watching from the gallery as you unroll the scroll, Nobuyori's face turns ashen.
273: You notice that Yoshitomo has lately been calling often at the In's palace to pay his respects, and keeps a polite distance from Nobuyori.
274: You fail to notice that Yoshitomo, Chief of the Left Stables, has lately been a frequent visitor at Nobuyori's mansion.
275: Emperor Nijō ascended the throne on the 11th day of the 8th month of Hōgen 3. For “a council of Buddha with Buddha,” see the Hyōhanki.
276: Shinzei's admonition by way of the Song of Everlasting Sorrow scroll is known from his colophon as quoted in the Gyokuyō.
277: Grant Nobuyori the Major Captaincy of the Inner Palace Guards
278: Shinzei will be furious, but Nobuyori will be yours body and soul
280: The historical path. Nobuyori nurses a grudge
281: Favour neither: hold an imayō banquet and seat the two together
286: On the 4th day of the 12th month, Kiyomori sets out with the young men of his house on pilgrimage to Kumano. The troops of Rokuhara go south with him, and the capital is left empty.
287: For days now, unfamiliar warriors have been coming and going outside Sanjō-dono. A man of the Northern Guard reports that crowds gather night after night at Nobuyori's mansion, and that the retainers of Yoshitomo, Chief of the Left Stables, pass in and out among them.
288: “My lord, Lord Nobuyori has invited me to rise with him. I have not agreed,” Yoshitomo says, his voice pitched low. “But I do not know how many more times I can refuse him.”
289: “The Lay Priest has been uneasy of late,” says Lady Kii, her face clouded with worry. “He says he has watched the heavens at night, and seen ill omens.”
290: Shinzei has heard the rumours too. But he is a man who trusts his own calculations too much.
291: On the timing of Kiyomori's Kumano pilgrimage, see the Heiji Monogatari and the Gukanshō. The Heiji Disturbance broke out while he was away from the capital.
292: Summon Kiyomori back to the capital at once, and secretly warn Shinzei to flee
293: Kiyomori may not arrive in time, but Shinzei might live
294: Arms ≥ 20, or Yoshitomo already generously rewarded
295: Pay it no mind; Shinzei can handle it himself
296: Secretly ally with Nobuyori, and use his troops to keep Shinzei in check
297: Shinzei has grown too strong. Perhaps he should be made to suffer a little
300: You give your tacit consent. Nobuyori bows low and takes his leave, saying: “Let my lord only sit at ease. Leave everything to me.”
301: That night, he and Yoshitomo surround Sanjō-dono with five hundred horsemen. They do not bow to you—soldiers shove your carriage aside and “invite” you into another, bound for the *Ippon-gosho-dokoro* in the Greater Palace. Sanjō-dono goes up in flames; the ladies-in-waiting who cannot escape throw themselves into the well, until the bodies choke its mouth.
302: Only now do you understand that “using his troops” and “being held by his troops” are separated by a single sheet of paper. Nobuyori never wanted to check Shinzei. He wanted to take his place.
303: Now you are the imperial seal in Nobuyori's hand.
304: This is a partially rewritten line. Historically, Go-Shirakawa was carried off to the Ippon-gosho-dokoro; whether he had any foreknowledge is unknown.
305: When Kiyomori returns to the capital, turn against Nobuyori
306: Turning coat requires Favor—and a Tengu's heart
308: He was once loyal to you
310: Deep in the night, hoofbeats draw near. Fujiwara no Nobuyori and Minamoto no Yoshitomo surround Sanjō-dono with more than five hundred horsemen and set fire to all four gates.
311: They push you into a carriage and take you under guard to the Ippon-gosho-dokoro in the Greater Palace—protection in name, imprisonment in fact. The ladies and attendants of the palace scatter and flee; many leap into the well, until it is filled layer upon layer. The flames in the Heiji Monogatari Emaki are the flames of this night.
312: Thanks to your secret warning, Shinzei slipped out of his mansion at Anegakōji-Nishinotōin before the fire began and hid in a temple near Rokuhara. He has survived.
313: Shinzei escaped in advance and fled to Tawara in Yamashiro, where he had his attendants dig a pit and buried himself in the earth, breathing through a bamboo tube. The pursuers found his hiding place; when they dug him out, he had already taken his own life. His head was hung on the tree at the prison gate in the capital.
314: Nobuyori appoints himself Major Captain of the Inner Palace Guards and holds a grand jimoku in the palace, rewarding his partisans. Yoshitomo becomes Governor of Harima, and his son Yoritomo Assistant Captain of the Right Military Guards—a boy of thirteen wearing court robes for the first time.
315: The Heiji Disturbance began on the night of the 9th day of the 12th month of Heiji 1. For Shinzei's death at Tawara and the display of his head, see the Heiji Monogatari and the Hyakurenshō.
316: Yoritomo's appointment as Assistant Captain of the Right Military Guards (Uhyōe-no-suke) at this time is the origin of his later title, “Suke-dono.”
317: Watch how things unfold, and say nothing
318: Secretly summon Kiyomori by In-zen to strike down the rebels
319: Have an attendant sew it into his collar and carry it out
323: Hearing of the uprising, Kiyomori hurries back from Kii and enters Rokuhara. On the one hand he sends Nobuyori a myōbu, a name-register, feigning submission; on the other he secretly reaches out to Emperor Nijō's close ministers, *Fujiwara no Tsunemune* and *Fujiwara no Korekata*.
324: Late on the night of the 25th, Emperor Nijō puts on women's robes and slips out of the palace in an ox-carriage, its blinds lowered. The warriors at the gate lift the blind to look, see only a “lady-in-waiting” with head bowed in silence, and let the carriage pass. The Emperor enters Rokuhara.
325: That same night, taking advantage of lax guards, you too quietly leave the Ippon-gosho-dokoro.
326: You look back once. Nobuyori is still sound asleep in the hall. He does not know his “jewel” has already rolled away of its own accord.
327: You hear horses neighing in the distance, from the direction of Rokuhara.
328: For Emperor Nijō's escape in women's dress and Go-Shirakawa's flight to Ninna-ji, see the Heiji Monogatari and the Gukanshō. Tsunemune and Korekata's defection to Kiyomori was decisive.
329: Slip away to Ninna-ji and wait for the outcome
330: The historical path. Siding with no one, you may advance or withdraw
331: Go straight to Rokuhara, and stand with the Emperor in Kiyomori's camp
336: On the 26th day of the 12th month, the Taira army counterattacks the Greater Palace, feigns retreat to lure Yoshitomo out, and retakes the palace. In the decisive battle on the riverbed at Rokujō, Yoshitomo is crushed and flees east with his sons.
337: Nobuyori flees to Ninna-ji and kneels before you, begging for his life. Kiyomori's soldiers arrive close behind and drag him out through the temple gate. On the 27th, Nobuyori is beheaded on the Rokujō riverbed.
338: In the 1st month of Eiryaku 1, Yoshitomo flees to Noma in Owari and takes shelter in the house of his old retainer Osada Tadamune. While he is in the bath, Osada and his son stab him to death. It is said that as he died he cried out: “If only I had a wooden sword!”
339: In the 2nd month, thirteen-year-old *Minamoto no Yoritomo* is captured in Ōmi and brought to Rokuhara. When Kiyomori's stepmother *Ike-no-Zenni* sees the boy, she says he is the very image of her own son Iemori, who died young, and day after day she weeps and begs Kiyomori to spare him. Your full elder sister *Jōsaimon-in* Muneko—whom Yoritomo once served as a chamberlain—also sends word pleading for him.
340: “My stepmother weeps and pleads with me every day. I truly do not know what to do.” Kiyomori comes to ask your mind. “What does the Cloistered Emperor— no, forgive me, the Retired Emperor—think?”
341: Yoshitomo's death at the hands of Osada Tadamune: see the Heiji Monogatari and the Gukanshō.
342: Ike-no-Zenni's plea for Yoritomo's life: see the Heiji Monogatari. Yoritomo had served Jōsaimon-in as her chamberlain (kurōdo).
343: Quietly assent to Ike-no-Zenni's plea, and exile Yoritomo to Izu
344: Argue for pulling the weed out by the roots
345: Kiyomori will heed his stepmother in the end, but your words will remain on record
346: Plead with Kiyomori in person, and give Yoritomo a sutra scroll
347: Through twenty years in Izu, he will remember this sutra
351: The Insult of the Viewing Stand
352: After the disturbance, Emperor Nijō's close ministers Tsunemune and Korekata grow ever more arrogant. Proclaiming “the Emperor's personal rule,” they pay you no regard at all.
353: You often visit the mansion of Fujiwara no Akinaga at Hachijō-Horikawa and watch the comings and goings of the street from its *sajiki*, a viewing stand—one of your few pleasures. One day, Tsunemune and Korekata have the sajiki boarded up, so that you can never look out again.
354: “In all this world,” you say before Kiyomori, tears actually falling, “you are the only one I can rely on.”
356: Were those tears performed? Even you cannot say.
357: For Tsunemune and Korekata's boarding of the sajiki and Go-Shirakawa's tearful appeal to Kiyomori, see the Gukanshō, Book 5. The two were soon arrested; Tsunemune was exiled to Awa, Korekata to Nagato.
358: Weep before Kiyomori, and have him arrest the two
360: A quarrel between Emperor and Retired Emperor should not be settled by warrior hands
361: Send the Northern Guard to seize the two yourself
362: The In has soldiers of his own
367: At Shichijō in the Eastern Hills you build a new palace called *Hōjūji-dono*. On the day it is finished you move in, and for the next thirty years it is from here that commands go out to the realm.
368: That autumn your beloved lady-in-waiting *Koben-dono*—daughter of Taira no Tokinobu, younger sister of Taira no Tokitada, and half-sister of Tokiko, Kiyomori's wife—bears you a son, named *Norihito*. Koben-dono is the later *Taira no Shigeko*, Kenshunmon-in.
369: Taira no Tokitada and Kiyomori's brother Norimori, beside themselves with joy, secretly plot to have Norihito made Crown Prince. Word leaks out; Emperor Nijō, enraged, strips both men of their offices on the spot.
370: Emperor and Retired Emperor, son and father, now stand openly opposed. Kiyomori, meanwhile, keeps on good terms with both: he stands night watch for the Emperor in the palace, and sends tribute from his estates to you at Hōjūji-dono. People say Kiyomori is 「アナタコナタ」 (“this way and that”)—courting both sides.
371: Prince Norihito (Emperor Takakura) was born on the 3rd day of the 9th month of Ōhō 1. On Tokitada and Norimori's dismissal for plotting to make him Crown Prince, see the Hyakurenshō and the Gukanshō.
372: The phrase 「アナタコナタ」 comes from the Gukanshō, describing Kiyomori's manoeuvring between Nijō and Go-Shirakawa.
373: Endure, and have Tokitada withdraw for a time
374: The historical path. Wait for the Emperor to come of age—or wait for the Emperor to…
375: Fight to have Norihito named Crown Prince
376: Nijō will surely strike back with the personal-rule faction
377: Go to the palace yourself, and speak to Nijō as a father to his son
378: He is, after all, your eldest son
382: On the 17th day of the 12th month, *Rengeō-in*, Kiyomori's offering, is completed. The main hall stretches more than a hundred and twenty metres north to south, with thirty-three bays between its pillars—hence its common name, Sanjūsangen-dō. Within it sit one seated Thousand-Armed Kannon and stand a thousand more, golden light filling the hall like a sea of gold.
383: Emperor Nijō attends the dedication in person. Father and son offer incense side by side before the hall, and the whole court breathes a sigh of relief.
384: You send an envoy inviting Emperor Nijō to attend, but the Emperor refuses to come. Weeping before the hall, you say to those around you: 「何の憎さに」 (“What is it he so hates?”)—what is there in me to hate?
385: In the 8th month of the same year, news comes from Shikoku: the Retired Emperor Sutoku has died in Sanuki.
386: Your brother lived out his natural span at Ninna-ji. Before he died he wrote you a waka, recalling the cherry blossoms of Hōkongō-in in your boyhood.
387: It is said that in his place of exile Sutoku spent three years copying the five Mahāyāna sutras in his own blood, and asked that they be dedicated at a temple in the capital. The court, suspecting a curse hidden within, refused them. Hearing this, it is said, Sutoku bit his tongue and wrote in blood at the end of the sutras: “I shall become the great demon of Japan; I shall make the sovereign a commoner, and the commoner a sovereign.” From then on he let his hair and nails grow uncut, and took on the living form of a Tengu.
388: Rengeō-in was completed on the 17th day of the 12th month of Chōkan 2. For Emperor Nijō's refusal to attend and Go-Shirakawa's complaint 「何の憎さに」, see the Gukanshō, Book 5.
389: The Retired Emperor Sutoku died in the 8th month of Chōkan 2. The tale of the five Mahāyāna sutras written in blood comes from the Hōgen Monogatari; it is the root of later vengeful-spirit legends, not established fact.
391: The historical path. The vengeful spirit will haunt the rest of your life
392: Dedicate the sutras at Anrakuju-in in Toba, and send an envoy to mourn at Shiramine
393: A scroll of sutras might yet bring a soul to rest
394: Hold the forty-ninth-day rites for your brother at Ninna-ji
395: In the end, you never met as enemies on the field
398: In Eiman 1, Emperor Nijō falls gravely ill and passes the throne to his infant son Nobuhito, still in swaddling clothes, who becomes *Emperor Rokujō*. Nijō dies soon after, at twenty-three. The personal-rule faction has lost its keystone.
399: In the 7th month of the next year, the young regent Fujiwara no Motozane dies suddenly. His wife is Kiyomori's daughter Moriko, just eleven years old. To whom should the Regents' house's generations of estates now pass?
400: In Nin'an 2, Kiyomori is raised to Junior First Rank and *Chancellor of the Realm*—a man of warrior birth at the very summit of the court, without precedent. Three months later he resigns and withdraws to Fukuhara in Settsu. In Nin'an 3, you have Rokujō abdicate in favour of eight-year-old Norihito, who becomes *Emperor Takakura*.
401: In the 6th month of Kaō 1, you shave your head at Hōjūji-dono, taking the Buddhist name *Gyōshin*, and are henceforth called the *Cloistered Emperor*. That same year, Otomae dies at past eighty.
402: As she lies dying, you go to her bedside yourself, chant the Lotus Sutra for her, and sing one of the old melodies she taught you. She holds your hand, her lips moving faintly, as if singing along.
403: You send offerings for her rites. From then on, the imayō banquets of the In's palace are missing a voice.
404: Emperor Rokujō ascended the throne in the 6th month of Eiman 1. Motozane died in the 7th month of Nin'an 1; his estates were inherited by Moriko and in effect passed to the Taira. See the Gukanshō.
405: Go-Shirakawa took the tonsure on the 17th day of the 6th month of Kaō 1, with the Buddhist name Gyōshin. For the year of Otomae's death and his visit to her deathbed, see the Ryōjin Hishō Kudenshū.
406: Accept Kiyomori's proposal, and let Moriko administer the Regents' estates
407: Return the Regents' estates to Motozane's brother Motofusa
408: The Fujiwara will be grateful to you
409: Declaring that “a child widow cannot manage them,” take them into the In's own domains
414: Kiyomori has built a villa at Fukuhara and improved the harbour at Ōwada-no-tomari, so that Song merchant ships can sail into the Seto Inland Sea. Song coins, incense and medicines, brocades, books—they flood in like the tide.
415: In the 9th month of that year, Kiyomori invites you to Fukuhara, saying that men of Song wish to be received.
416: “Behold, Your Cloistered Majesty—celadon from Song, coins from Song. With these, what need have we to depend on the estates of the provinces?”
417: “Such a thing has not happened in our realm since the Engi era. Is it the work of the Heavenly Demon?”—so Kujō Kanezane writes in his diary, the Gyokuyō.
418: In the 7th month of the same year, another incident occurs: the attendants of the Regent Motofusa quarrel on the road with the carriage train of Kiyomori's grandson Sukemori, and beat and humiliate him. In the 10th month, Taira warriors ambush Motofusa's procession and shear the topknots of his attendants in disgrace. This is the *Denka Noriai*, the Regent's Carriage Incident. Kiyomori's grandson can now humiliate the reigning regent.
419: Go-Shirakawa's reception of Song visitors at Fukuhara: see the Gyokuyō, entry for Kaō 2, 9th month, 20th day.
420: For the Denka Noriai, see the Gyokuyō and The Tale of the Heike. The Tale of the Heike blames Kiyomori, though another account holds that Shigemori was in fact responsible.
421: Receive the Song guests yourself, and admire the wonders of Song
422: The historical path. The In's domains and the Taira alike will grow rich on Song coin
423: Use Song coin to recruit warriors of the home provinces lavishly, and strengthen the In's Northern Guard
425: Politely decline, and have Kiyomori receive them in your stead
426: The Regents' house and the nobles will praise your prudence
429: At Hōjūji-dono, a banquet of strings and winds is under way. Fan in hand, beating time, you sing with your favourites as the merriment reaches its height.
430: Suddenly a monk bursts into the courtyard, his voice like a great bell, unrolls a subscription list, and reads it aloud: *Jingo-ji* at Takao has long lain in ruin, and the Cloistered Emperor is asked to donate an estate for its restoration.
431: Everyone is aghast. The music stops. When the guards step forward to drive him out, the monk fights back with his fists, injuring several, still cursing without pause: “The Emperor's banquet is not worth a single roof tile of a temple of the Buddha!”
432: His name is *Mongaku*, in lay life Endō Moritō, once a man of Jōsaimon-in's Northern Guard. It is said that in his youth he took holy orders after mistakenly killing the woman he loved, Kesa Gozen, and practised austerities beneath the Nachi waterfall, more than once on the brink of death.
433: For Mongaku's intrusion into Hōjūji-dono and his exile to Izu, see The Tale of the Heike, Book 5, “Kanjinchō.” In Izu, Mongaku came to know Yoritomo.
434: Punish him for his insolence, and exile him to Izu
435: The historical path. There is another exile in Izu
436: Laugh aloud, grant his request, and donate an estate
437: Even a mad monk has his uses
441: You and Kenshunmon-in board the imperial ship together and set out from Fukuhara across the Seto Inland Sea on pilgrimage to Itsukushima Shrine in Aki.
442: The great vermilion torii stands in the sea; when the tide comes in, the whole shrine seems to float upon the waves. Kiyomori welcomes you here and shows you the Heike Nōkyō—sutras copied in the hands of thirty-two members of his house, painted in gold and silver, magnificent beyond compare.
443: Three years ago, Kiyomori's daughter *Tokuko* entered the palace as your *yūshi*, your adopted daughter, married Emperor Takakura, and was made Empress. Takakura is your son; Tokuko is your adopted daughter. The Taira and the imperial house are, for now, one family.
444: These years are the best you and Kiyomori will ever have. Kenshunmon-in stands between you, like a silk thread, fine and unbreaking.
